concept.name: Gross domestic product
concept.definition: The total value of the final goods and services produced within a country during a given period. In the United States it is estimated quarterly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis as the signature measure of the National Income and Product Accounts.
concept.intuition: GDP is the economy's scoreboard: it tells you how much the country actually produced in a quarter or year, and its growth rate is the standard gauge of whether the economy is expanding or contracting.
concept.mechanics: BEA sums spending on final goods and services (consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports), counting only final output to avoid double-counting intermediates. Each quarter is estimated three times (advance, second, third) as more source data arrive, and figures are seasonally adjusted and reported at annual rates.
concept.formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), where C = personal consumption expenditures, I = gross private domestic investment, G = government consumption and investment, X = exports, M = imports (expenditure approach).
concept.failure_modes: GDP is revised repeatedly, so the first estimate traders react to can change materially; it is also backward-looking, ignores non-market activity and income distribution, and annualized quarterly rates can exaggerate one-off swings.
concept.misconceptions: GDP does not measure well-being or total wealth, and a high GDP level does not imply strong growth; what markets trade on is the growth rate relative to expectations, not the level.
concept.example: When BEA reported Q1 2020 GDP falling at a 5.0% annual rate, it confirmed the pandemic contraction; traders compared each release against consensus to reprice Fed policy expectations.

citations.source: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center)
